body.heading: A code written in four letters
paragraphs: DNA — deoxyribonucleic acid — is the molecule that stores the instructions for building and running a living thing. It is shaped like a twisted ladder, the double helix, whose rungs are made of four chemical letters: A, T, C and G, always pairing A with T and C with G.

The order of those letters is the information. A stretch of DNA that carries one complete instruction is called a gene, and most genes tell the cell how to build one particular protein — the molecules that do almost all the work in a body.

body.heading: From instructions to proteins
paragraphs: Cells cannot build proteins directly from DNA, so they copy the needed gene into a messenger molecule, RNA, which travels out of the nucleus. There, ribosomes read the copy three letters at a time and assemble a chain of amino acids in exactly the order the gene specifies.

Folded into its final shape, that chain becomes a working protein: haemoglobin to carry oxygen, insulin to manage sugar, or an enzyme to speed up a chemical reaction. Change one letter in a gene and the protein may change too — the root of many inherited conditions.

body.heading: Three billion letters in every nucleus
paragraphs: Your full instruction book, the human genome, holds about three billion letter pairs, divided among 46 chromosomes in almost every cell. Unravelled and stretched out, the DNA from a single cell would measure about two metres.

Yet roughly 98 per cent of it does not code for proteins at all. Much of that remainder switches genes on and off, deciding why a nerve cell and a skin cell — carrying identical DNA — do completely different jobs.

takeaway: DNA stores life's instructions as a four-letter code; genes are the individual instructions, read by cells to build proteins.
